title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression
claim: Training loss collapses early while test loss stays high for orders of magnitude more steps before eventually vanishing, in both linear and nonlinear models.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared log x-axis, shaded variance bands
description: Two side-by-side line plots with dashed grid lines share a logarithmic x-axis labeled training steps (10^0 to 10^6) and a y-axis labeled square loss. In each, a red training-loss curve falls steeply and reaches near zero by about 10^3 steps. A blue test-loss curve declines slowly, plateaus around 0.15–0.2 through 10^4, then drops to zero near 10^5. Shaded bands show variability across 50 runs: pink for training, purple-blue for test, and wide at the start. Both panels have a legend in the upper right. The left panel is ridge regression and the right is a two-layer ReLU network. The eye goes to the large gap between the red and blue curves.
caption: Comparing training and test squared losses using GD with weight decay over 50 independent runs (with independent datasets and student initializations). Left: training a ridge regression model to learn the zero teacher; Right: training a two-layer ReLU neural network (training both layers) to learn the zero teacher. We scale the x-axis logarithmically, which is commonly adopted for plotting the grokking phenomenon [ref]. See Section [ref] for further details of the experimental setup.
abstract: We study grokking, the onset of generalization long after overfitting, in a classical ridge regression setting. We prove end-to-end grokking results for learning over-parameterized linear regression models using gradient descent with weight decay. Specifically, we prove that the following stages occur: (i) the model overfits the training data early during training; (ii) poor generalization persists long after overfitting has manifested; and (iii) the generalization error eventually becomes arbitrarily small. Moreover, we show, both theoretically and empirically, that grokking can be amplified or eliminated in a principled manner through proper hyperparameter tuning. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first rigorous quantitative bounds on the generalization delay (which we refer to as the "grokking time") in terms of training hyperparameters. Lastly, going beyond the linear setting, we empirically demonstrate that our quantitative bounds also capture the behavior of grokking on non-linear neural networks. Our results suggest that grokking is not an inherent failure mode of deep learning, but rather a consequence of specific training conditions, and thus does not require fundamental changes to the model architecture or learning algorithm to avoid.
